title: Thirteen Weeks Out: Why October Is the Right Time to Bring In Fractional CFO Support Before Christmas
linkedin:
Thirteen weeks from today lands in the third week of January.

That one number covers both the Christmas trading peak and the quiet month that follows it, in a single stretch, instead of two separate surprises most businesses live through every year.

Here's the pattern we see across owner-led businesses: the decision to bring in financial leadership almost always gets made reactively. Cash goes tight, a lender asks a question nobody can answer quickly, or growth outpaces the finance function. All legitimate reasons. But by the time that decision gets made, the lead time to actually prepare for what's coming has usually already been spent.

Christmas trading isn't a surprise. Stock, casual wages and marketing spend all land before the revenue does, which is exactly the kind of timing mismatch that makes a profitable quarter feel like a cash-poor one. January isn't a surprise either. Trading slows, staff are back from leave, and BAS, super and lease commitments don't pause just because revenue has.

When a fractional CFO partnership starts in late October, the first few weeks go into understanding the ledger and building a rolling cash view, often structured like a 13-Week Cash Flow Build, rather than a static budget nobody revisits after March. Starting now means that forecast is live and tested before either swing lands, not assembled in a hurry once the first supplier invoice arrives early.

None of this needs a crisis to justify it. It just needs the calendar.

A quick bit of calendar maths worth sitting with this week: thirteen weeks from today lands in the third week of January. For a lot of owner-led businesses across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria, that stretch covers two of the biggest swings of the trading year in one go, the Christmas rush and the quieter month that tends to follow it.

Most businesses meet these as two separate surprises each year. Stock, casual wages and marketing spend go out before the Christmas revenue lands, which can make a genuinely profitable quarter feel cash-poor. Then January slows down just as BAS, superannuation and lease payments keep arriving on schedule.

The businesses that handle both periods comfortably usually aren't the ones with the biggest pipeline. They're the ones who had a cash flow view in place before either swing started, not partway through it. Late October, with thirteen weeks of runway left, is a sensible point in the year to build that view if you haven't already.
